ecological-systems.def: Bronfenbrenner’s theory that a child develops within nested systems: the microsystem (family, school), mesosystem (links between them), exosystem (settings that affect the child indirectly), macrosystem (culture, laws) and chronosystem (change over time).

parenting-style.def: A parent’s general approach to raising a child, combining how warm and responsive they are with how many rules and demands they set.

authoritarian.def: A parenting style with strict rules, little explanation and little warmth ("Because I said so").

authoritative.def: A parenting style that combines warmth with clear, explained rules and listens to the child; linked with good outcomes in many US studies.

permissive.def: A parenting style that is warm but sets few rules or limits and makes few demands.

temperament.def: A person’s inborn, partly heritable style of emotional reactivity and activity, such as easygoing, fussy or slow to warm up, visible from infancy.

attachment.def: A deep emotional bond between a child and a caregiver, shown by seeking closeness and by distress at separation.

strange-situation.def: Ainsworth’s laboratory procedure in which a 1-year-old is briefly separated from and reunited with a caregiver in an unfamiliar room; the child’s behavior, especially at reunion, classifies attachment.

secure-attachment.def: An attachment pattern in which a child explores using the caregiver as a safe base, may be upset at separation, and is readily comforted at reunion.

avoidant-attachment.def: An attachment pattern in which a child shows little distress at separation and ignores or turns away from the caregiver at reunion.

anxious-attachment.def: An attachment pattern (also called anxious-ambivalent) in which a child is very upset at separation and both clings to and resists the caregiver at reunion.

disorganized-attachment.def: An attachment pattern in which a child shows confused or contradictory behavior with the caregiver, such as freezing or approaching while looking away.

separation-anxiety.def: An infant’s distress when separated from a familiar caregiver, typically appearing around 8 months and peaking in the second year.

contact-comfort.def: The comfort an infant gets from soft physical touch; Harlow’s monkeys showed it matters more than feeding for forming attachment.

parallel-play.def: Play in which young children (often around age 2) play side by side with similar toys but with little interaction.

pretend-play.def: Make-believe play in which children use objects and actions to stand for something else, such as a block as a phone; it blossoms in the preschool years.

psychosocial-stages.def: Erikson’s eight stages of life, each with a social challenge: trust versus mistrust, autonomy versus shame and doubt, initiative versus guilt, industry versus inferiority, identity versus role confusion, intimacy versus isolation, generativity versus stagnation, and integrity versus despair.

identity-status.def: Marcia’s four ways of approaching identity, by whether a person has explored options and made commitments: achievement (both), moratorium (exploring), foreclosure (committed without exploring) and diffusion (neither).

imaginary-audience.def: A teenager’s belief that others are watching and judging them far more than they really are.

personal-fable.def: A teenager’s belief that their experiences are unique and that they may be invulnerable to risks that affect others.

social-clock.def: A culture’s expected timing for life events such as leaving home, marriage, parenthood and retirement.

emerging-adulthood.def: A period from about 18 to the mid-20s, common in wealthy countries, when many people have left adolescence but have not yet taken on full adult roles.

aces.def: Adverse childhood experiences: stressful events in childhood such as abuse, neglect or a household member’s substance use, mental illness or incarceration; more ACEs are linked to higher average health risks in adulthood.

possible-selves.def: The images people hold of who they might become, both hoped-for and feared, which can motivate present behavior.
